name: What This Means for Each Reader
title: What This Means for Each Reader
answer: This idea explains what AI readiness means for each group in a school community: teachers should test AI on their own workload first, leaders should decide which tools are approved and how data is handled, board members should ask oversight questions, and parents should ask what tools their child uses and whether the child can explain the work. It matters because each role has a different decision to make, and the thinking must stay with the student.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: The idea sets out a division of responsibility so that AI enters a school deliberately rather than by accident. Teachers begin with their own tasks, such as drafting a parent email or practice questions, so they discover the tool's strengths and weaknesses before students rely on it. Principals and district leaders decide which tools are approved, what data may go into them, and who owns each decision. School board members oversee rather than choose tools, asking what problem AI solves and how the district will know it worked. Parents ask which tools their child uses and what happens to what the child types in. The problem it solves is confusion over who decides what, and the risk that AI quietly does the learning instead of the student.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, a teacher uses an approved school tool to draft a parent email, a set of practice questions, or a reading passage at a lower level, then checks and edits the result. This lets the teacher learn where the tool helps and where it stumbles before students ever touch it. When students do use AI, the assignment is designed so the thinking stays with them. For leaders, the work is to decide which tools are approved, what data may go into them, and who owns each decision, then train staff before rolling anything out and measure results before scaling. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so the same approach applies across year levels.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers a policy landscape rather than a research finding. It states that as of June 2026, somewhere between 35 and 37 states plus Puerto Rico had issued AI guidance for schools, depending on who is counting, and that Ohio went further by requiring every district to adopt an AI policy by July 1, 2026, citing Playlab, 2026, and the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, 2026. It also refers to the Los Angeles story as showing why a board's questions about vendors and data matter as much as its questions about learning. The text does not present a study or measured outcome for the practice itself, so the guidance rests on practice and policy rather than research evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by role. Teachers must check and edit whatever the tool produces, and they must design assignments so the thinking stays with students. Leaders must decide approved tools, permitted data, and decision ownership, train staff before rollout, and measure results before scaling. Board members should not select tools, only ask what problem AI solves, how the district will know it worked, what student data goes in and where it goes, and which decisions a person will still make. Parents should ask which tools their child uses and what happens to the information typed in, and at home the useful test is whether the child can explain the work in their own words. The text also notes that many tools have age limits and parental consent rules, which later chapters list for each product.
